quote: it is for exactly this reason, I suggest, that he introduces phantasia: to preempt charges that he cannot explain the possibility of error himself
claim: Aristotle introduces phantasia to preempt charges that he cannot explain the possibility of error

quote: For this strategy to work, he must show first that phantasia is distinct from sensation and conception
claim: For Aristotle's strategy to succeed, he must demonstrate that phantasia is distinct from sensation and conception

quote: secondly that, unlike those states, its content genuinely does admit of error. That is precisely what the remaining sections of De anima 3.3 set out to do
claim: Aristotle must show that phantasia's content admits of error, unlike sensation and conception, and this is what De anima 3.3 demonstrates

quote: Phantasia, then, is crucial for Aristotle's account of intentionality - his account of how mental states can be of or about things, or more generally possess content
claim: Phantasia is crucial for Aristotle's account of intentionality (how mental states possess content about things)

quote: Sensation and conception are, of course, intentional states. But they do not provide Aristotle with a model that will explain intentionality in general
claim: Sensation and conception are intentional states but do not provide a model explaining intentionality in general

quote: the content of most intentional states can fail to correspond to what is in the world; and his account of sensation and conception precludes just such divergence
claim: Most intentional states' content can fail to correspond to the world, but Aristotle's account of sensation and conception precludes such divergence

quote: he is also confident that phantasia can explain the possibility of error, and he regularly appeals to it in explaining the content of other intentional states
claim: Aristotle is confident phantasia can explain error and regularly appeals to it when explaining other intentional states' content

quote: De anima 3.3 thus testifies to Aristotle's concern with problems arising from intentionality and his effort to solve them
claim: De anima 3.3 testifies to Aristotle's concern with intentionality problems and his effort to solve them

quote: The first half of the treatise is foundational, consisting of a review of his predecessors' opinions (1. 1-1 .5) and the definition of the soul (2.1-2.3)
claim: The first half of De anima is foundational: review of predecessors' opinions and definition of the soul

quote: It then ascends through the basic powers of the soul, insofar as they divide living things into three successive kingdoms
claim: De anima ascends through basic soul powers that divide living things into three successive kingdoms

quote: first, the capacity for digestion, growth, and reproduction (2.4), the sole powers found in plants; secondly, the capacity for perception (2.5-3.2), which animals possess in addition
claim: Plants have only nutritive powers; animals additionally possess perception

quote: finally, conceptual and reasoning powers (3.4-3.8), which humans alone possess, along with all the other powers
claim: Humans alone possess conceptual and reasoning powers in addition to all other powers

quote: The sequence of chapters thus mirrors the hierarchy Aristotle finds in the soul and in nature at large
claim: The sequence of De anima chapters mirrors Aristotle's hierarchy in soul and nature

quote: He leaves until afterwards the discussion of other powers, such as desire and action (3.9-3.1 1), that mark no important taxonomic distinction
claim: Aristotle discusses desire and action afterwards because they mark no important taxonomic distinction

quote: Phantasia breaks this pattern. It also belongs to every (or almost every) animal. But it is not dealt with afterwards like the others
claim: Phantasia breaks De anima's structural pattern: it belongs to almost all animals yet is not treated afterwards like desire and action

quote: coming instead at the critical juncture between perception and thought, in De anima 3.3
claim: Phantasia is discussed at the critical juncture between perception and thought in De anima 3.3

quote: The placement of this chapter might be nothing more than an accident of composition or the work of later editors
claim: One possibility is that De anima 3.3's placement is accidental or due to later editors

quote: we cannot discount another possibility, namely, that phantasia is somehow necessary at this stage of Aristotle's exposition, prior to his accounts of thought, desire, and action
claim: An alternative possibility is that phantasia is necessary prior to Aristotle's accounts of thought, desire, and action

quote: Instead of interrupting the sequence, De anima 3.3 might constitute an integral part of it
claim: De anima 3.3 may constitute an integral part of the treatise's sequence rather than an interruption

quote: Aristotle is sensitive to the question of continuity himself in this chapter
claim: Aristotle is sensitive to the question of continuity in De anima 3.3

quote: [People] define soul by two differentia most of all: (i) change in place and (ii) conceiving, thinking, and perceiving
claim: Soul is commonly defined by two differentia: change in place and conceiving/thinking/perceiving

quote: In the De anima, the criteria of motion and perception form a leitmotiv. Introduced near the beginning of the treatise, they are sounded throughout the first book
claim: The criteria of motion and perception form a leitmotiv throughout De anima

quote: So revised, the two criteria neatly foreshadow the treatise's two remaining topics of thought and action
claim: The revised two criteria foreshadow De anima's remaining topics of thought and action

quote: Aristotle only says here that thought seems to be like perception. It is a reputable view or ?vbooov, from which it is appropriate to start
claim: Aristotle presents the view that thought seems like perception as an endoxon (reputable view) to start from

quote: The first third of De anima 3.3 is a concerted attack to show that thought is crucially not like perception, in a way that requires a distinct new ability, like phantasia
claim: The first third of De anima 3.3 attacks the view that thought is like perception, showing a distinct ability like phantasia is required

quote: And the argument turns precisely on the problem of error
claim: The argument distinguishing thought from perception turns on the problem of error

quote: thinking and perceiving are both cognitive attitudes. In each case, he notes, "the soul discriminates and knows something that is"
claim: Aristotle notes that thinking and perceiving are both cognitive attitudes where the soul discriminates and knows

quote: "in addition, the ancients say that thinking and perceiving are the same"
claim: Aristotle claims the ancients said thinking and perceiving are the same

quote: The evidence Aristotle provides for this historical claim, though, seems frail
claim: The evidence Aristotle provides for his historical claim about the ancients seems frail

quote: None of these citations mentions perception, and the second in its original context is not about thinking either, but dreams
claim: None of Aristotle's citations mentions perception, and the second (Empedocles B 108) originally concerns dreams, not thinking

quote: At most, these citations share the very general position that a person's thoughts depend in some way on his environment and on his bodily condition
claim: At most, the citations show only that thoughts depend on environment and bodily condition

quote: But that hardly amounts to an identification of thinking with perception. Even the ancient commentators are openly critical
claim: The citations do not amount to an identification of thinking with perception; even ancient commentators are critical

quote: Aristotle's appeal to inference is a silent admission that he can only defend a more modest claim: that his predecessors are committed to the thesis
claim: Aristotle's appeal to inference admits he can only defend that predecessors are committed to the thesis, not that they explicitly stated it

quote: if his inference is to be valid, this thesis must only maintain that (1) Thinking consists in the same kind of process as perceiving
claim: For Aristotle's inference to be valid, the thesis must be that thinking consists in the same KIND of process as perceiving (not strict identity)

quote: rather than the strict identity claim that (I') Thinking does not differ from perceiving in any way at all
claim: The thesis is not the strict identity claim that thinking does not differ from perceiving in any way

quote: Theophrastus, who observes that Empedocles took thinking and perceiving to be "either the same or nearly the same"
claim: Theophrastus reports Empedocles took thinking and perceiving to be 'either the same or nearly the same'

quote: Two things cannot be "nearly identical." But they can be nearly the same sort of thing
claim: Two things cannot be 'nearly identical' but can be nearly the same sort of thing, supporting the weaker reading

quote: (2) Thinking and perceiving are both bodily processes (3) One thinks and perceives like by like
claim: Aristotle attributes to predecessors two reasons: (2) thinking and perceiving are both bodily, and (3) like is known by like

quote: Though each is a sufficient condition for (1), neither (2) nor (3) is a necessary condition
claim: Each reason (bodily process, like by like) is sufficient but not necessary for thesis (1)

quote: the question arises as to how widely Aristotle intends his remarks to extend - in particular, whether his critique is aimed at (1) quite generally
claim: It is unclear whether Aristotle's critique targets thesis (1) generally or only when combined with (2) and/or (3)

quote: He directs our attention to the widespread phenomenon of error and challenges his predecessors to account for it
claim: Aristotle directs attention to the widespread phenomenon of error and challenges predecessors to account for it

quote: Yet at the same time they should have said something about being in error, too, since this is particularly endemic to animals
claim: Aristotle argues predecessors should have addressed error since it is particularly endemic to animals

quote: Aristotle taunts his predecessors for not discussing error precisely because he thinks they cannot - theories like theirs do not have sufficient resources to explain error
claim: Aristotle taunts predecessors for not discussing error because their theories lack resources to explain it

quote: It is necessary either that (i) all appearances are true (as some have said); or that (ii) contact with what is unlike is error
claim: Aristotle argues predecessors must hold either (i) all appearances are true or (ii) error is contact with what is unlike

quote: his predecessors must either (i) forestall the problem at the outset, by simply denying that error ever occurs
claim: Option (i) forestalls the problem by denying error ever occurs

quote: (ii) offer the only model their theory seems to allow, one in which a mental state occurs, but not in the way required - when some sort of malfunction occurs
claim: Option (ii) explains error as malfunction - mental state occurring but not in the required way

quote: If like is known by like, though, this could only occur when unlikes interact
claim: On the 'like by like' theory, error could only occur when unlikes interact

quote: I thus disagree both with Modrak... when she claims that Aristotle does not have a general account of intentionality
claim: Caston disagrees with Modrak's claim that Aristotle lacks a general account of intentionality

quote: and with Modrak... when she argues that Aristotle offers just such an account in his theory of sensation
claim: Caston also disagrees with Modrak's view that Aristotle's general intentionality account is in his theory of sensation

quote: in the De anima Aristotle is in fact committed to strict coextension - i.e., phantasia belongs to every animal, including stationary animals
claim: In De anima, Aristotle is committed to phantasia belonging to every animal, including stationary ones

quote: given that there cannot be desire of any sort on his view without phantasia (3.10, 433b28-29), these claims together imply that all animals have phantasia
claim: Since desire requires phantasia and all animals have desire, all animals have phantasia

quote: the dilemma is meant to be acceptable. Aristotle intends each as a reductio ad absurdum
claim: Aristotle intends each horn of the dilemma as a reductio ad absurdum

quote: In the first half of the Theaetetus, Socrates examines the thesis (A) that knowledge is perception - a close relative of (1)
claim: Socrates in the Theaetetus examines the thesis that knowledge is perception, which is closely related to thesis (1) about thinking and perceiving

quote: argues that it is inextricably linked to the thesis (B) that all appearances are true, as well as to something he calls the "Secret Doctrine,"
claim: In the Theaetetus, the thesis that knowledge is perception is linked to (B) all appearances are true and (C) the 'Secret Doctrine' about perception existing only in subject-object interaction

quote: Adherence to this last doctrine is practically universal, Socrates argues - "with the exception of Parmenides, all the sages one after another agree about this"
claim: Socrates claims nearly universal adherence to the Secret Doctrine among ancient sages, excepting Parmenides

quote: if, as Myles Burnyeat has argued, they are supposed to mutually imply each other
claim: Burnyeat argues that doctrines (A), (B), and (C) in the Theaetetus are supposed to mutually imply each other

quote: Plato may have believed that adherence to (A), the thesis that knowledge is perception, committed his predecessors to (B), the thesis that all appearances are true
claim: Plato may have believed that accepting knowledge-is-perception commits one to the thesis that all appearances are true

quote: Like Aristotle, then, he might also have believed that widespread accounts of thought were unable to account for error
claim: Both Plato and Aristotle may have believed that widespread ancient accounts of thought could not account for error

quote: Aristotle's interests here are primarily psychological, not epistemological: knowledge and justification are not even on the table yet
claim: Aristotle's interests in De anima 3.3 are primarily psychological rather than epistemological; knowledge and justification are not yet at issue

quote: Instead of the "Secret Doctrine," Aristotle appeals to more prosaic premises, such as (2) and (3); and his conclusion is not that all appearances are true - that is only one horn of his dilemma
claim: Aristotle appeals to simpler premises than Plato's Secret Doctrine, and concludes only that 'all appearances are true' is one horn of a dilemma, not his final conclusion

quote: In Aristotle's eyes, the first horn is a complete nonstarter. He offers no further argument against it here, but is content to stand on the assertion that error is, in fact, prevalent
claim: Aristotle regards the first horn (that all appearances are true) as a complete nonstarter and offers no further argument, relying on the evident prevalence of error

quote: In Metaphysics 4.5, for example, Aristotle recognizes that some sort of rebuttal may be felt necessary, even though proof in the strict sense is impossible over so fundamental a principle
claim: In Metaphysics 4.5, Aristotle recognizes that some rebuttal of denials of error may be needed even though strict proof is impossible for such a fundamental principle

quote: psychology is not the place for such arguments. Error is a datum that must be accounted for if a theory is to count as a psychological theory at all
claim: Error is a datum that any psychological theory must account for; psychology is not the place to argue for the existence of error

quote: his own theory must be measured against this desideratum, too. Aristotle cannot afford to be smug if he cannot solve the problem himself
claim: Aristotle's own theory must also be measured against the desideratum of accounting for error

quote: By itself, the thesis that (1) thinking and perceiving are the same sort of process hardly implies infallibility
claim: Thesis (1) that thinking and perceiving are the same sort of process does not by itself imply infallibility

quote: But (2), the thesis that thinking and perceiving are bodily processes, is not of much help either. It is unclear (to say the very least) how the corporeality of a process could imply its infallibility
claim: Thesis (2) that thinking and perceiving are bodily processes does not help explain infallibility; corporeality does not imply infallibility

quote: he takes many corporeal processes to be subject to error
claim: Aristotle takes many corporeal processes to be subject to error

quote: It is rather (3), the thesis that one thinks and perceives like by like, that leads to the dilemma
claim: It is thesis (3) — that one thinks and perceives like by like — that leads to the dilemma about error

quote: when the Presocratic citations are taken in context, it is evident that 'perceiving' and 'thinking' do not stand for two isolated processes, but rather all mental states
claim: In context, 'perceiving' and 'thinking' in the Presocratic citations denote all mental states, not just two isolated processes

quote: (3) runs together two issues which are rarely distinguished in ancient discussions - indeed, one upshot of De anima 3.3 is precisely that a successful psychology must distinguish them
claim: Thesis (3) conflates two issues rarely distinguished in ancient discussions; one upshot of De anima 3.3 is that successful psychology must distinguish them

quote: the claim that one knows "like by like" addresses two quite different questions: first, how a certain mental state is brought about; and second, what the resulting state is about, i. e., what its content is
claim: The 'like by like' principle addresses two distinct questions: (1) how mental states are caused, and (2) what the content of those states is

quote: An object is known because it interacts with something in the subject "like" itself. A mental state will consequently be about what brings it about
claim: On the 'like by like' view, an object is known because it interacts with something like itself in the subject, so mental states are about their causes

quote: That (3) is, in part, a thesis about content is usually masked by the emphasis given to the causal half of the story
claim: That thesis (3) is partly about content is typically obscured by the emphasis placed on its causal component

quote: On Empedocles' view, for example, a person sees a fire when effluences of fiery material flowing from a fire find their way into the eye and meet the fiery material enclosed there
claim: On Empedocles' view, seeing fire involves fiery effluences from fire entering the eye and meeting fiery material already present there

quote: what determines the content of this state - what makes it a case of seeing the fire - is that there is actually something present in the eye exactly like this original cause
claim: For Empedocles, the content of a visual state is determined by the presence in the eye of something exactly like the external cause

quote: 'Content' is no metaphor here. A mental state, on Empedocles' view, is about X only when something like X is contained, literally, inside of us
claim: For Empedocles, 'content' is literal: a mental state is about X only when something like X is literally contained inside us

quote: (3) thus marries content to cause. A mental state arises whenever an object interacts in the appropriate way, specifically when like affects like; and the resulting mental state will be about its cause
claim: Thesis (3) marries content to cause: mental states arise through interaction of likes, and their content is their cause

quote: (3a) One perceives or thinks whenever like is affected by like (3b) Whatever one perceives or thinks on a given occasion corresponds exactly to whatever brings that state about
claim: Thesis (3) can be reformulated as two subtheses: (3a) cognition occurs when like affects like; (3b) content corresponds exactly to cause

quote: considered in themselves, (3a) and (3b) are logically independent of one another - it is possible to accept one without being committed to the other
claim: Subtheses (3a) and (3b) are logically independent; one can accept either without being committed to the other

quote: Someone might, for example, reject (3a), while accepting (3b) on other grounds; in fact, on Aristotle's interpretation, that is exactly Anaxagoras' position
claim: On Aristotle's interpretation, Anaxagoras rejects (3a) while accepting (3b) on other grounds

quote: from (3b) alone, it trivially follows that (4) Whatever one perceives or thinks on a given occasion corresponds exactly to something in the environment
claim: From (3b) alone it follows trivially that (4) content corresponds exactly to something in the environment, since causes must exist

quote: on Aristotle's view, they will exist at the same time as well
claim: On Aristotle's view, causes and effects exist at the same time

quote: Such correspondence, though, clearly precludes error
claim: Exact correspondence between content and external cause precludes the possibility of error

quote: Propositional attitudes, such as believing that p, will be brought about by that very state of affairs, p; while nonpropositional attitudes, such as thinking about X or desiring X, will be brought about by that stuff, property, or individual, X
claim: On (3b), propositional attitudes are brought about by the state of affairs they represent; nonpropositional attitudes by the objects they are about

quote: The content of these states cannot diverge from reality. If this thesis applies to all mental states, error will be impossible
claim: If (3b) applies to all mental states, content cannot diverge from reality and error becomes impossible

quote: (3), that is, would imply that (5) All appearances are true just as the first horn of the dilemma states
claim: Thesis (3) implies (5) that all appearances are true, which is the first horn of the dilemma

quote: One cannot accept a completely general reading of (3) and hold that error is possible, on pain of contradiction
claim: Accepting a completely general reading of (3) while holding error possible leads to contradiction

quote: To allow for the existence of error, then, an adherent of (3) must restrict its scope
claim: To allow for error, an adherent of (3) must restrict its scope

quote: The only way to do this, while preserving the general character of the thesis, would be to say that (3) applies to all and only veridical mental states
claim: The only way to preserve (3)'s general character while allowing error is to restrict it to veridical mental states only

quote: once we have added the restriction to veridical states, (5) only amounts to the tautology that all veridical appearances are true
claim: With the restriction to veridical states, (5) becomes the tautology that all veridical appearances are true

quote: The proponent of this restricted version of (3) no longer has a fully general explanation of content, which (3) used to provide, so there is a lacuna in his story that needs to be filled
claim: The restricted version of (3) loses its general explanation of content, creating a lacuna requiring an alternative account

quote: He cannot explain the content of the remaining states through the interaction of likes without falling back on the first horn
claim: Nonveridical states cannot be explained through interaction of likes without returning to the first horn

quote: provided that these states occur as the result of some sort of interaction, it follows that they must be due to the interaction of unlikes - just as Aristotle says in the second horn
claim: Nonveridical states, if caused by interaction, must be due to interaction of unlikes — the second horn of the dilemma

quote: The dilemma Aristotle invokes is thus a genuine one, brought about by thesis (3), that like is known by like, when this is understood as a thesis about mental states in general
claim: The dilemma Aristotle invokes is genuine and arises from thesis (3) when understood as applying to all mental states

quote: Unlike the first horn, Aristotle cannot just rule the second one out as absurd. It acknowledges the existence of error and attempts to account for it
claim: Aristotle cannot rule out the second horn as absurd because it acknowledges error and attempts to explain it

quote: If he rejects it, it can only be because he believes it to be false; and that requires argument
claim: Aristotle's rejection of the second horn requires argument since it is not obviously absurd

quote: But both error and knowledge of contraries seem to be the same. (427b5-6)
claim: Aristotle's compressed objection states: error and knowledge of contraries seem to be the same

quote: This is not Aristotle's own view, of course - it is extremely unlikely he believes any instances of error and knowledge are the same - but something he takes to follow from the second horn
claim: The claim that error and knowledge coincide is not Aristotle's own view but something he takes to follow from the second horn as a reductio

quote: his argument constitutes a simple reductio ad absurdum: if error were due to the interaction of unlikes, then error and knowledge would coincide in the case of contraries; but error and knowledge never coincide
claim: Aristotle's argument is a reductio: if error is due to interaction of unlikes, then error and knowledge would coincide for contraries; but they never coincide; therefore error is not due to interaction of unlikes

quote: The difficulty, of course, lies in the first inference. How, given this model of error, could error and knowledge coincide?
claim: The difficulty in Aristotle's argument lies in explaining how error and knowledge could coincide given the unlike-interaction model

quote: Knowledge always involves a pairing of likes on this account, error a pairing of unlikes. But such pairings never coincide, even when we consider contrary objects
claim: On this account, knowledge involves pairing likes and error pairing unlikes, but these pairings never coincide even for contraries

quote: As it stands, the second horn of the dilemma remains unscathed
claim: Without additional premises, the second horn of the dilemma remains unrefuted

quote: Modern commentators such as Hicks and Ross have been tempted to add a premise which Aristotle shares with the Academy, namely, that "the knowledge of contraries is the same"
claim: Hicks and Ross propose adding the Academic premise that 'knowledge of contraries is the same' to complete Aristotle's argument

quote: as this gloss makes clear, the reconstruction appeals to a different sense of episteme. The opening of De anima 3.3 is not concerned with knowledge as a subject-area (i. e., scientia, Wissenschaft), but as a kind of mental act
claim: The Hicks-Ross reconstruction uses the wrong sense of 'episteme'; De anima 3.3 concerns knowledge as a mental act, not as a subject-area

quote: To obtain the requisite sense, we need a slightly different claim, such as we find in Nicomachean Ethics 5.1, when Aristotle asserts that "a contrary state is often recognized from its contrary"
claim: The relevant premise is from Nicomachean Ethics 5.1: a contrary state is often recognized from its contrary

quote: One part of the contrariety is sufficient to discriminate both it and what corresponds to it. For by means of the straight we recognize both it and the curved
claim: According to De anima 1.5, one part of a contrariety suffices to discriminate both it and its contrary (e.g., the straight enables recognition of both straight and curved)

quote: For Aristotle's purposes, a single counterexample will do
claim: For Aristotle's reductio, a single counterexample of knowing one contrary from another suffices

quote: Once this is added as a tacit premise - e. g., that we know the unhealthy by means of the healthy - then his reductio is valid
claim: With the tacit premise that we know one contrary by means of the other (e.g., unhealthy by healthy), Aristotle's reductio becomes valid

quote: Since it involves an interaction of unlikes, on his opponents' view it will also be a case of error. But then it follows that it is both a case of knowledge and a case of error, which is absurd
claim: Knowing one contrary from another involves interaction of unlikes, so on opponents' view it would be both knowledge and error, which is absurd

quote: Aristotle's opponents are free, of course, to deny the premise which has been smuggled in. But Aristotle would not be troubled over it
claim: Aristotle's opponents could deny the tacit premise, but Aristotle would not be troubled since he considers it independently reputable
